**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0550), Paper 2, ORDINARY LEVEL, JUNE 2021. Duration: TWO AND A HALF (2 1/2) HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR Questions choosing ONE from each section.

Questions ONE carries 30 marks. All the other Questions carry 20 marks each.

Each question that is sub-divided has the sub marks in brackets.

In questions involving calculations, all steps of the working MUST be shown.

If an outline MAP and/or GRAPH are used, they must be tied inside your answer booklet, opposite the written part of the answer.

NB - ONLY THE FIRST FOUR QUESTIONS ANSWERED WILL BE MARKED.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
1. Study the Ordnance Survey Map Extract of Waddington, (1:50 000) and answer the following questions:

![fig-1](gce-ol-geography-2021-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

*Ordnance Survey 1:50 000 map extract of Waddington (grid eastings 94 to 02 across the bottom, northings 52 to 65 up the side). The sheet supplied with the paper was printed with north to the right; it is turned here so that north is at the top.*

(a) (i) Describe the nature of the landscape in grid square **9658**. (2 marks)

(ii) State:

- Four human features found in grid reference **9856**.
- The height of the highest point in square **9760**.

(4+2 = 6 marks)

(b) On a graph paper, draw a cross section along northing **60** from **940600** to **020600** and annotate:

(i) A 15 trunk road,

(ii) railway cutting,

(iii) river Brant,

(iv) electricity transmission line.

Give the section an appropriate title and vertical scale of **1 cm: 20m**

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Method (follow these steps and show them on the graph paper).**

1. **Length of the section.** Northing 60 runs from 940600 (easting 94.0) to 020600 (easting 02.0), that is **8 km**. At 1:50 000, 1 cm on the map is 0.5 km, so the base line is **8 km / 0.5 km per cm = 16 cm** long. Draw a horizontal line 16 cm long on the graph paper (the horizontal scale is 1:50 000, which you must state).
2. **Vertical scale.** The scale is given: **1 cm : 20 m**. The highest ground along the line is a little under 80 m, so the vertical axis must reach at least 80 m, i.e. 4 cm (use 5 cm, 0 to 100 m). Label the axis every 20 m. (The vertical exaggeration is (1 cm : 20 m) compared with (1 cm : 500 m), that is 25 times.)
3. **Transfer the information.** Lay the edge of a strip of paper along northing 60. Mark on it the start (940600), the end (020600), the position of each feature, and the position and height of every contour line that touches the edge (contours are every 10 m). Place the strip on the base line of the graph and mark a dot at each position at the correct height (height / 20 = height in cm). Join the dots with a smooth line.
4. **Annotate** the four required features at their positions along the line (the eastings are read from the map and are approximate):
   - **River Brant**: at about easting 94.3, in the low ground at the west end of the section (the valley floor, about 5 to 8 m);
   - **Electricity transmission line** (line of pylons): at about easting 96.05, i.e. near 960600;
   - **Railway cutting** (the hatched symbol of the dismantled railway): at about easting 96.9, i.e. near 969600, shown as a small notch in the profile;
   - **A15 trunk road**: at about easting 01.2, i.e. near 012600, in the east, where the height is about 48 m.
5. **Title and labels:** "Cross section along northing 60 from 940600 to 020600 (Waddington map extract, 1:50 000)", horizontal scale 1:50 000 (1 cm = 0.5 km), vertical scale 1 cm : 20 m, labelled axes (eastings and heights in metres), neat and in pencil.

**The model profile.** The section starts on very low ground (about 5 to 10 m) at the River Brant, rises very gently to about 20 m near the railway, then climbs steeply (a steep west-facing slope with closely spaced contours) to a crest of roughly 75 to 80 m between eastings 98 and 99 (the village of Coleby and the A607 lie on this slope and crest), and then falls gently eastwards to about 50 m at the A15.

![fig-2](gce-ol-geography-2021-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

*The heights on this model are approximate readings (to within about 10 m, one contour interval) taken from the faint contours of the scanned map; on the real map you must read every contour.*

**Marks (8).** Title (1); horizontal scale and base line of the right length (1); vertical scale and axes labelled in metres (2); accurate profile (2); the four features correctly placed and annotated (2).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) State the direction of the church in Coleby (**975607**) from the church in Harmston (**975624**).

(2 marks)

(ii) Calculate the distance along the electricity transmission lines from (**962598**) to (**991597**).

(2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Direction.** Both churches have the same easting, **975**, so one is exactly above the other. Coleby church (northing **607**) has a smaller northing than Harmston church (northing **624**), so it lies **south** of it. The direction of the church in Coleby from the church in Harmston is **due South** (bearing 180 degrees on the grid; the two churches are 1.7 km apart, since 62.4 km - 60.7 km = 1.7 km).

**(ii) Distance along the electricity transmission line.** The line of pylons runs almost straight from 962598 to 991597.

- Change in easting: 99.1 km - 96.2 km = 2.9 km.
- Change in northing: 59.8 km - 59.7 km = 0.1 km (negligible).
- Distance = $\sqrt{2.9^2 + 0.1^2} = \sqrt{8.42} \approx 2.90$ km.

**Measuring on the map:** the line is about 5.8 cm long and the scale is 1 cm = 0.5 km, so the distance is 5.8 cm x 0.5 km/cm = **2.9 km** (answers from 2.8 to 3.0 km are acceptable).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) (i) Compare the settlement of Waddington and Leadenham under the headings: size, shape and functions.

(2+2+2 = 6 marks)

(ii) Comment on the distribution of woodland in the map.

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Waddington and Leadenham (2 + 2 + 2 marks).** Both settlements lie at the edge of the map extract (Waddington at the top, Leadenham at the bottom left), so only the part shown can be compared.

| Heading | Waddington | Leadenham |
|---|---|---|
| **Size** | Large: a built-up area more than 1 km across, with many buildings and streets, still continuing beyond the north edge of the map. A large village or small town. | Much smaller: a built-up area well under 1 km across (the part shown), with far fewer buildings. A village. |
| **Shape** | Nucleated (compact), roughly rectangular, with a dense network of roads and many short cul-de-sac streets, showing modern planned estates; the main road passes along its western side. | Elongated (linear) along the main road, with a small cluster at a road junction; the lines of the roads that meet there give it a long, narrow shape. |
| **Functions** | Mainly residential. It has services (post office, public houses, public buildings) and a nearby **airfield** to the east (a military and aviation function). | Mainly residential and a service village for the farms around it (post office, public house, an "Old Hall"); an agricultural function with little industry. |

**Conclusion:** Waddington is the larger, compact and more varied settlement; Leadenham is the smaller, linear, mainly residential and agricultural village.

**(ii) The distribution of woodland (4 marks).**

- Woodland (shown in green; pale yellow-green on this scan) covers **only a very small part** of the area. There are no large forests.
- It is found as **small, scattered patches**: copses and coverts (for example Fox Covert and Gorse Covert), a plantation (Cocked Hat Plantation) and one larger block, **Green Man Wood**, at the eastern edge of the map. A thin strip of plantation lies in the west, near Harmston Field.
- The patches are **isolated and irregular in shape**, mostly **in the east and the south**, and more often on the higher ground and the heathland than on the low land of the west.
- The **centre and the north** are almost without woodland: most of the land is open arable farmland divided into fields, with the villages and roads, which suggests that the trees were cleared for farming and that the small woods were kept for game, shelter or timber.
